q: Does the hybrid HHL++ resource reduction (fewer 2q gates, flat qubit cost) hold when the input matrix A is sparse-but-non-Hermitian or non-trivially structured, rather than the small dense Hermitian matrices used in the paper's Table 1 and this replication?
basis: The paper and this replication only test small dense Hermitian systems with exact-in-binary eigenvalue phases. Real linear-system workloads (PDE discretizations, network Laplacians, finance covariance) are typically sparse with irrational eigenvalues that don't align to n-bit clock precision, and non-Hermitian A requires a dilation step that adds qubits.
next_steps: Generate a stratified matrix suite: (i) tridiagonal Poisson-1D at n=8/16/32, (ii) random sparse Hermitian with density 0.1 and controlled kappa in {5,10,50}, (iii) block-Hermitian dilations of random non-Hermitian systems. Re-run baseline vs hybrid HHL for each, report qubit / CNOT / depth curves + fidelity vs numpy.linalg.solve. Threshold: hybrid resource-reduction claim survives iff CNOT reduction stays >=50% and fidelity stays >=0.95 across the suite.

q: Can hybrid HHL++ be composed with modern block-encoding / qubitization primitives (e.g. Low-Chuang) to achieve better asymptotic scaling in kappa and sparsity than either technique alone?
basis: The paper's semiclassical-QPE saving is essentially a classical-precomputation crutch that flattens the QPE register; block-encoding attacks a different axis (linear-combination-of-unitaries structure and kappa dependence). Whether the two savings compose or one dominates is not addressed in the paper.
next_steps: Implement a Qiskit prototype where the hybrid HHL's eigenvalue-inversion block is replaced with a QSVT/qubitization-based matrix-inversion primitive. Compare 2q-gate count and success probability vs (a) pure hybrid HHL and (b) pure QSVT inversion on the same 8x8 sparse Hermitian instance. Metric: whether the combined circuit shows sub-additive resource growth in (kappa, 1/epsilon).

q: How robust is the hybrid step (the mid-circuit-measurement + classical feed-forward + gamma-scaling selection) to realistic gate + measurement noise on today's superconducting hardware (IBM Heron / Google Willow), as opposed to the trapped-ion Quantinuum H-series the paper measured?
basis: Quantinuum H-series has substantially better mid-circuit-measurement fidelity than most superconducting platforms (H-series specs ~99.7% MCM vs superconducting typically 97-99%). The paper's Table 2 hardware fidelities (98.6% at 3-bit falling to 42.6% at 5-bit) are H-series-specific; the hybrid's classical-feedback loop may amplify MCM error on lower-fidelity platforms.
next_steps: Run the hybrid HHL circuits from the paper's Sec.4 on IBM Heron (via free Qiskit Runtime open-plan queue) at 3-bit and 4-bit precision, using dynamic circuits for the mid-circuit measurement. Report success probability and solution fidelity vs the noiseless statevector reference. Compare degradation slope vs the paper's Quantinuum Table 2 slope.

q: Does hybrid HHL++ provide an actual end-to-end speedup on a specific real-world PDE or finance instance (e.g. 128-node Poisson-1D, 32-asset mean-variance portfolio) once state-preparation cost for |b>, tomography / amplitude-estimation cost for extracting x, and repeated-sampling overhead from post-selection are all counted?
basis: HHL's asymptotic O(log N) advantage is famously eroded by state-prep + readout + repetition. The paper reports circuit resources but not the full end-to-end resource budget for a target-accuracy solution vector on a specific instance; the hybrid saving may be dwarfed by prep+readout.
next_steps: Pick one concrete instance (128-node 1D Poisson with known analytic solution). Cost out: (a) state-prep for |b> via Grover-Rudolph or unary encoding, (b) full hybrid-HHL inversion, (c) amplitude estimation to recover each component of x to fixed epsilon=0.01, (d) repetition factor from post-selection probability. Compare total-2q-gate budget vs a classical CG solve. Report as a break-even (N, epsilon) plot.

q: Can a small classical-ML preconditioner (e.g. graph-neural-net predicting a good clock-register scaling gamma from the matrix A directly) close the fidelity gap at higher clock precision (5-bit and above), where the paper's Table 2 shows fidelity collapsing to 42.6% at 5-bit on real hardware?
basis: The paper's gamma-selection algorithm (Sec.3) is a hand-designed classical procedure. An ML-learned gamma predictor could in principle exploit matrix-structure patterns the hand-designed rule misses, and the 5-bit hardware-fidelity collapse suggests headroom.
next_steps: Generate a training set of ~500 random small (2x2 to 8x8) Hermitian A's with paired optimal-gamma labels from an exhaustive sweep. Train a simple MLP or small GNN to predict gamma from A's eigenvalue histogram / spectral gap. Compare hybrid HHL fidelity using ML-predicted gamma vs paper's hand-designed gamma across a held-out test set at n_clock in {3,4,5}. Threshold: ML variant wins iff mean 5-bit fidelity improves by >=10 percentage points.
